title: Public health coding with R
text:
Welcome
This is an exercise book for SPH5009 at the NUS Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health. Each numbered section corresponds to a week of the course. Contents are being dynamically built and adjusted as our course progresses to reflect the learnings in class.

title: Public health coding with R
section: Setup before first day of class
text:
Setup before first day of class
Follow these instructions in Section 1.1 to install R and Rstudio. Once installed, check out Section 1.2 to familiarize yourself with the Rstudio interface. Seek help here if you face difficulties.
That’s it! Breathe deep and enjoy the ride as we cruise through the exercises in class together. You will do great!

title: Feeling at home with R
text:
Welcome to Week 1 of Public health coding with R. At this point, you should have both R and Rstudio installed, ready to go.
Let’s open up Rstudio. Recap the four panes:

Console. An R session where your code will run.
Source. A text editor where you can open (multiple) text files, your scripts.
Environment. Lists of objects in your R environment.
Files, plots, packages, help (stacked tabs).


Arrange your panes however feels comfortable. Many people put Source top-left and Console bottom-left, so you can see your script and its output at the same time. You can rearrange this under Tools > Global Options > Pane Layout.


Working Directory
Every R session has a working directory: the folder on your computer that R treats as “home base” while it runs. When you tell R to read a file, save a file, or load data using just a filename (no full path), R looks for that file in the working directory, or saves it there.
You can check your current working directory at any time with:
getwd()
This prints the full path of the folder R is currently using. It’s a good habit to run getwd() whenever you’re unsure why R can’t find a file you know exists, since the file may simply be sitting in a different folder.

Working directory: The default folder R uses to look for and save files when you don’t specify a full file path.



Project Directory
Instead of setting your working directory manually every time with setwd(), we’ll use an RStudio Project. A project locks your working directory to a specific folder, so file paths stay consistent no matter who runs the script or where the folder lives on disk.

Avoid using setwd("C:/Users/yourname/Desktop/...") in your scripts. It only works on your computer, with your folder structure. If you share the script, it will break for anyone else. Projects solve this problem for you.

Create a new project now: File > New Project > New Directory > New Project. Give it a name and pick a location you’ll remember.


Create Your First Script

Go to File > New File > R Script.
Save it as week1.R inside your project folder.
Check the Files pane: does week1.R show up? If not, make sure you’re working inside your project directory.


Script: A plain text file (ending in .R) where you write R code that can be saved, edited, and rerun later, as opposed to typing directly into the Console, which is not saved.



Sending Code from Script to Console
Type the following in your script:
1 + 1
Place your cursor on that line and press Ctrl+Enter (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Enter (Mac) to run it. The line gets sent to the Console and the result appears there.

You’ll use Ctrl+Enter / Cmd+Enter constantly. Get comfortable with it now, since it’s much faster than retyping code into the Console by hand.

You can also leave yourself notes in a script using #. Anything after a # on a line is ignored by R:
# This is a comment. R will not run this line.
1 + 1


Simple Arithmetic
Try running each of these lines one at a time:
5 + 3
5 - 3
5 * 3
5 / 3
5 ^ 3
5 %% 3

%%: The modulo operator, it returns the remainder after division. For example, 5 %% 3 returns 2, because 3 goes into 5 once with a remainder of 2.



Creating Your First Object
x = 5
Check the Environment pane: you should see x appear with the value 5.

Object: Anything you create in R (a value, vector, function, etc.) and store with a name, so you can refer to it again later.

For historical reasons, R can assign values using <- (an arrow) or ->. You’ll also see = used for assignment, which is the common convention across most other programming languages, and what we’ll use in this course.
x = 5     # what we'll use in this course
x <- 5    # equivalent, historically the more "R-idiomatic" way
5 -> x    # also equivalent, less common

All three do the same thing here. Pick one and be consistent, don’t worry about which is “more correct.” That debate is older than most of us and not worth your time right now.

You can print an object’s value by typing its name alone:
x

x = 5 creates an object silently, it does not print anything to the Console. If you want to see the value, run x on its own line, or wrap the assignment in parentheses: (x = 5).



Vectorized Thinking
Create a vector using c() (short for “combine”):
nums = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
nums * 2
Notice that nums * 2 multiplied every element by 2, without a loop.

Vectorized operation: Applying an operation to an entire vector at once, element by element, without writing an explicit loop. This is a core feature of R and one of the biggest mental shifts if you’re coming from Excel or another language.


Exercise 1.1

Create a numeric vector of 5 numbers of your choice.
Add 10 to the whole vector at once. What do you get?
Multiply the vector by itself (nums * nums). What happened, element by element?
crumbs: 2  Feeling at home with R

title: Data Types
text:
Every object you create in R has a data type. The data type determines what kind of values an object can hold, and what operations make sense on it: you can add two numbers together, but adding two pieces of text doesn’t mean anything the same way. Knowing an object’s data type helps you understand what R will let you do with it, and helps you spot bugs when something doesn’t behave the way you expect.

Vectors
Vectors are data types with one-dimension where all elements in the vector are of the same type. R has several basic vector types:

character: text, e.g. "hello"
numeric: decimal numbers, e.g. 3.14
integer: whole numbers, e.g. 5L
logical: TRUE / FALSE
factor: categorical data with fixed levels, e.g. "low", "medium", "high"

char_vec = c("apple", "banana", "cherry")
num_vec = c(1.5, 2.7, 3.9)
int_vec = c(1L, 2L, 3L)
log_vec = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
fac_vec = factor(c("low", "high", "medium"), levels = c("low", "medium", "high"))

L suffix: Writing 5L tells R to store the value as an integer rather than a numeric (double). Without the L, a whole number like 5 is stored as numeric by default. In practice the distinction rarely matters for day-to-day analysis, but you’ll see L used when a function specifically expects an integer (e.g. nrow, or arguments like nrow = 2L in some packages).


NA: R’s representation of a missing value. It can appear inside any vector type (e.g. c(1, 2, NA, 4)) and will show up often once you start working with real data.



Checking Data Types
class(char_vec)
str(fac_vec)
length(num_vec)

class(): Tells you what type an object is. str(): Gives you a compact summary of an object’s structure. length(): Tells you how many elements are in it.



Accessing Elements
char_vec[1]        # by position
names(num_vec) = c("a", "b", "c")
num_vec["b"]        # by name

R indexing starts at 1, not 0. char_vec[1] gives you the first element, not the second.



Matrix
A matrix is a 2-dimensional structure where every element must be the same type (usually numeric).
m = matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
m
dim(m)
m[1, 2]     # row 1, column 2

Matrix: A rectangular grid of values, all of the same data type, arranged in rows and columns.


Naming Rows and Columns
You can give a matrix row names and column names when you create it, using the dimnames argument, or by setting rownames() and colnames() afterward:
m2 = matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3,
            dimnames = list(c("row1", "row2"), c("col1", "col2", "col3")))
m2

# equivalently
m3 = matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
rownames(m3) = c("row1", "row2")
colnames(m3) = c("col1", "col2", "col3")
m3
Once named, you can index by name instead of position:
m2["row1", "col2"]   # single element, by row name and column name
m2["row2", ]           # entire row, by row name
m2[, "col3"]           # entire column, by column name

Naming rows and columns makes your code more readable and less fragile: m2["row2", ] is much clearer than m2[2, ], and it keeps working even if you later reorder the rows.




List
A list can hold elements of different types and lengths, even other lists.
my_list = list(name = "Alice", age = 25, scores = c(90, 85, 88))
my_list$name
my_list[["scores"]]

List: A flexible container that can hold objects of different types and sizes together, accessed using $ (by name) or [[ ]] (by name or position).


You won’t use matrix and list constantly in this course, but you’ll see them show up under the hood (a data frame is technically a special kind of list!). It’s worth recognizing them when you see them.



Data Frame
A data frame is the structure you’ll use the most, think of it as a spreadsheet: rows are observations, columns are variables, and different columns can hold different types.
df = data.frame(
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol"),
  age = c(25, 30, 22),
  passed = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)
df
df$age          # access a column by name
df[1, ]         # access a row by position

Data frame: A table-like structure where each column can be a different data type, but all columns must have the same number of rows. In fact, a data frame is a special kind of list: each column is an element of the list, and the requirement that makes it a data frame (rather than a plain list) is that every element must have the same length.


Exercise 1.2

Create one of each fundamental data type (character, numeric, integer, logical, factor). Check each with class(), str(), and length().
Create a small matrix with matrix() and access one element using [row, col].
Create the same matrix but with row names and column names, and access the same element using its row name and column name instead.
Create a small list with at least two different types of elements and access one using $ or [[ ]].
Create a data frame with at least 2 columns and 3 rows. Access a single column and a single row.

title: Functions
text:
You now have stored some values as data objects and learnt how to perform simple arithmetic. Now, imagine you want to do something more complex, or something you’ll need to repeat many times. Retyping the same steps over and over is slow and error-prone. Functions solve this: they package up a set of instructions under a name, so you can reuse them by calling that name, often with different inputs each time.
Functions in R typically come from one of three sources:

Base R: functions that come built into R itself, available the moment you open RStudio, no extra installation needed.
Packages: functions written by the R community and shared as installable add-ons, extending what base R can do.
Your own functions: custom functions you write yourself, for steps specific to your own project or analysis.

We’ll look at all three in turn.

Base R
R has many built-in (“base”) functions organized by the type of data they work on.
Character functions:
nchar("hello")
substring("hello world", 1, 5)
paste("hello", "world")
paste0("hello", "world")
toupper("hello")
tolower("HELLO")
Numeric functions:
round(3.14159, 2)
floor(3.7)
ceiling(3.2)
abs(-5)
sqrt(16)
exp(1)
log(10)
log10(100)
log2(8)

Not sure what a function does or what arguments it takes? Type ?function_name in the Console, e.g. ?round. The Help pane will show you the documentation, including examples.



Packages
R ships with deliberately conservative set of commonly useful fucntions. Packages extend R with additional functions written by the community. Later in the exercise you’ll install tidyverse, a large collection of packages for data manipulation and visualization. For now, let’s install and try just one small package on its own, stringr, which provides functions for working with text (strings).
install.packages("stringr")
library(stringr)
stringr functions all start with str_, and do many of the same things as the base R character functions above, often with more consistent behavior and easier-to-read names.
str_detect("hello world", "world")               # does the string contain "world"?
str_replace("hello world", "world", "there")     # replace first match
str_pad("7", width = 3, pad = "0")                # pad to a fixed width, default pad = " "

Argument: A value you pass into a function to control what it does. Default value: A value an argument uses automatically if you don’t specify one yourself. In str_pad("7", width = 3, pad = "0"), width and pad are both arguments, and we’ve overridden pad’s default (which is a space, " ") with "0".


Look up ?str_pad in the Help pane. Every help page follows a similar structure, worth knowing how to read:

Description: A short summary of what the function does.
Usage: Shows how the function is called, including every argument and its default value, if it has one.
Arguments: Explains each argument in detail, what it expects and what it controls.
Value: Describes what the function returns.
Examples: Runnable code showing the function in action, usually the fastest way to understand a new function.



install.packages("stringr") downloads and installs the package (only needs to be done once per computer). library(stringr) loads it into your current session (needs to be done every time you restart R). Confusing these two is one of the most common early stumbling blocks.



Write Your Own Function
Sometimes no existing function does exactly what you need, this is when you write your own. The basic syntax is:
function_name = function(argument1, argument2 = default_value) {
  # code using argument1 and argument2
  return(result)
}
Here’s a simple example:
is_even = function(x = 2) {
  x %% 2 == 0
}

is_even(4)      # TRUE
is_even(7)      # FALSE
is_even()       # uses default argument value, x = 2, so TRUE

return(): Explicitly specifies what value a function sends back when it’s called. If you omit return(), R will automatically return the value of the last line evaluated inside the function, this is why is_even() above works even without an explicit return().


Arguments with default values (like x = 2 above) can be left out when calling the function, R will just use the default. Arguments without a default value must be supplied, or R will throw an error.


Exercise 1.3

Write a function that takes a number and returns whether it is “even” or “odd” (as text, not TRUE/FALSE).
Install and load the stringr package. Confirm library(stringr) runs without error. If it throws an error, flag your instructor.
Install and load the full tidyverse package (this may take a few minutes the first time). Confirm it runs without error. You’ll notice tidyverse loads stringr among several other packages, this is because tidyverse is a bundle of many smaller packages installed together.



Congrats! You have covered the fundamentals of R in one hour! Don’t worry. You don’t have to know them by heart now. Through repeated use, it will infuse into you in no time.

title: Data importation
text:
Setting up your data folder
First, let’s create a folder named data in your working directory to store all the data files, which you will download from Canvas (or from the links below, generated for this book).
dir.create("data")
Download these four files and move them into your local data folder: data.txt, data.tsv, data.csv, and data.xlsx.
Check the Files pane in RStudio. You should see a new data folder appear inside your working directory, containing the four files. If they don’t show up, click the refresh icon at the top of the Files pane.

title: Data importation
text: If the data folder or files don’t show up where you expect, double-check you’re looking inside your project folder, not some other location on your computer. This is exactly the kind of confusion that RStudio Projects and a consistent working directory are meant to prevent.

title: Data importation
text:
Base R import functions
Base R ships with several functions for reading plain-text data, with no extra packages required.


readLines() reads a text file line by line into a character vector. It doesn’t know anything about columns or delimiters — it’s the most “raw” way to bring text into R, useful for logs, unstructured text, or files you want to parse yourself.

lines <- readLines("data/data.txt")
lines



read.table() is the general-purpose workhorse for delimited files. You tell it the separator (sep = "\t" for tab-delimited, sep = "," for comma-delimited, etc.), and it returns a data.frame. Its defaults are geared toward “traditional” R usage: strings are sometimes converted to factors (depending on R version/options), and column names may be mangled to valid R names unless you tell it otherwise.

df_tsv <- read.table("data/data.tsv", sep = "\t", header = TRUE)
str(df_tsv)



read.csv() is simply read.table() with sensible defaults baked in for comma-separated files (sep = ",", header = TRUE). It’s the function most people reach for first when reading a .csv in base R.

df_csv <- read.csv("data/data.csv")
str(df_csv)

title: Data importation
text:
Tidyverse import functions
The tidyverse (via the readr and readxl packages) offers analogous functions with a more consistent, predictable, and faster implementation.


read_csv() (from readr) reads comma-separated files into a tibble rather than a base data.frame. Tibbles print more compactly, never auto-convert strings to factors, guess column types explicitly (printing a helpful message about what it guessed), and preserve column names exactly as they appear in the file (including spaces, if any).

library(readr)
df_csv_tv <- read_csv("data/data.csv")
df_csv_tv



readxl::read_excel() reads Excel spreadsheets (.xls or .xlsx) directly, without needing Excel installed or any conversion step. You can specify which sheet and which cell range to read, which is handy when a workbook has multiple tabs or extra header rows.

library(readxl)
df_xlsx <- read_excel("data/data.xlsx")
df_xlsx



A note on the :: notation
You may notice code like readxl::read_excel() instead of just read_excel(), and writexl::write_xlsx() instead of just write_xlsx(). The double-colon :: is R’s namespace operator: package::function() tells R exactly which package a function should come from, without requiring you to load that package with library() first.
This is useful for a few reasons:


Clarity. Writing readxl::read_excel() makes it immediately obvious, just by reading the code, which package a function belongs to — handy when you’re skimming a script months later or reading someone else’s code.

Avoiding conflicts. Sometimes two different packages define a function with the same name (for example, both dplyr and stats have a function called filter()). Using :: lets you pick exactly the one you want instead of relying on whichever package was loaded most recently (and therefore takes priority).

One-off use. If you only need a single function from a package, and don’t want to load the whole package (which can be slow, or can clutter your environment with functions you don’t need), :: lets you call it directly, as we do above with readxl::read_excel() and writexl::write_xlsx(), without ever running library(readxl) or library(writexl).

By contrast, for readr, we did run library(readr) before calling read_csv() — this is a stylistic choice. Both approaches are valid: use library() when you’ll be calling many functions from a package throughout your script, and use :: when you only need a function once or twice, or want to be explicit about where it’s coming from.
Base R vs. tidyverse: what’s the difference?
Both families ultimately produce a rectangular table you can work with in R, but they differ in a few practical ways: base R functions (read.table, read.csv) return a data.frame and historically default to converting character columns to factors and “cleaning” column names, whereas tidyverse functions (read_csv, read_excel) return a tibble, keep strings as strings by default, are generally faster on large files, and print explicit messages about the column types they’ve guessed so you can catch parsing mistakes early. Neither is “more correct” — base R functions have no dependencies beyond R itself (useful for portable scripts or package development), while tidyverse functions are often preferred in interactive data analysis for their speed and safer defaults.

Exercise 1.4

Import data.csv using read.csv() (base R) and again using read_csv() (tidyverse). Compare the classes of the two objects with class().
Import data.tsv using read.table(), making sure to set the correct sep argument.
Import the spreadsheet data.xlsx using readxl::read_excel().
Explore any one of the imported datasets with head(), tail(), summary(), nrow(), ncol(), dim(), and str(). Note down what each function tells you about the data.

title: Data visualisation
text:
Plotting systems in R
R doesn’t have just one way to make plots — three major systems coexist, and you’ll likely encounter all of them in the wild.

title: Data visualisation
text:
Base R graphics work out of the box, with no packages required. Functions like plot() and hist() are available the moment you open R. They’re quick for exploratory work, but customizing them (legends, colors, layering) can get verbose.

lattice is a package (also bundled with base R installations) designed around the idea of trellis graphs — plots automatically split into panels by one or more grouping variables. It predates ggplot2 and is still used in some statistical packages’ example code, but has mostly been superseded by ggplot2 for everyday use.

ggplot2 is the most popular modern plotting package, and comes bundled with the tidyverse. It implements the “grammar of graphics,” where a plot is built by layering components (data, aesthetics, geometries, scales, facets, themes) rather than issuing one big plotting command. This makes complex plots more consistent and reusable, at the cost of a small learning curve up front.

title: Data visualisation
text:
Simple base R plots
Base R gives you a handful of functions that you compose together, adding to the same plot rather than layering it as separate objects.


plot() is the general-purpose function for scatterplots (and more). For two numeric vectors, it draws points by default.

plot(viz_data$height, viz_data$weight,
     xlab = "Height (cm)", ylab = "Weight (kg)",
     main = "Height vs. weight")









points() adds more points to an existing plot, without starting a new one — useful for overlaying a second group.

plot(viz_data$height[viz_data$group == "Control"],
     viz_data$weight[viz_data$group == "Control"],
     col = "blue", xlab = "Height (cm)", ylab = "Weight (kg)",
     xlim = range(viz_data$height), ylim = range(viz_data$weight))
points(viz_data$height[viz_data$group == "High dose"],
       viz_data$weight[viz_data$group == "High dose"],
       col = "red")








lines() adds connected line segments to an existing plot — handy for trend lines or time series.

abline() draws a straight line across the whole plot, often used to add a reference line or a fitted regression line (e.g., abline(lm(weight ~ height, data = viz_data))).

plot(viz_data$height, viz_data$weight,
     xlab = "Height (cm)", ylab = "Weight (kg)")
abline(lm(weight ~ height, data = viz_data), col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)









hist() draws a histogram of a single numeric vector, automatically choosing bins (which you can override with the breaks argument).

hist(viz_data$response,
     main = "Distribution of response scores",
     xlab = "Response")

title: Data visualisation
text:
ggplot2
Unlike base R, where each function call adds to a running plot, ggplot2 builds a plot as a single object, with each + adding a new layer or setting. This means you can save an incomplete plot to a variable, then keep amending it later — a very different mental model from base R’s “draw, then annotate” approach.

library(ggplot2)

Simple plots (geoms)
Each geom_*() function draws a different kind of layer, and you combine data, aesthetics, and one or more geoms with +:


geom_point() for scatterplots.

geom_line() for connected line plots (typically over time or an ordered x-axis).

geom_bar() for bar charts where ggplot counts rows for you (one bar per category).

geom_col() for bar charts where you already have the bar heights as a column in your data.

geom_histogram() for histograms of a continuous variable.

geom_density() for a smoothed density curve, often used as a continuous alternative to a histogram.

geom_tile() for heatmap-style tiles, typically mapping a third variable to fill color across two categorical/continuous axes.


ggplot(viz_data, aes(x = height, y = weight)) +
  geom_point()








ggplot(viz_data, aes(x = response)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20)








ggplot(viz_data, aes(x = outcome)) +
  geom_bar()








aes() for aesthetics
The aes() function maps variables in your data to visual properties of the plot: color and fill control outline and fill colors (useful for distinguishing groups), alpha controls transparency (useful when points overlap), size and stroke control point size and outline thickness, and linewidth and linetype control the thickness and dash pattern of lines.

ggplot(viz_data, aes(x = height, y = weight, color = group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2)







Grouping and faceting
Sometimes you want one plot with groups distinguished by color (via aes(group = ...), color, or fill), and sometimes you want groups split into entirely separate panels:


facet_wrap() splits a plot into panels based on one variable, wrapping panels into a grid.

facet_grid() splits a plot into a grid of panels based on one or two variables (rows and/or columns).


ggplot(viz_data, aes(x = outcome, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ group)








ggplot(viz_data, aes(x = outcome, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_grid(site ~ group)







Tweaking the looks


Themes (e.g., theme_minimal(), theme_bw(), theme_classic()) change the overall visual style of a plot — background, gridlines, fonts — without touching the data or geoms.

Scales (e.g., scale_color_manual(), scale_x_continuous(), scale_fill_brewer()) control how data values map to visual properties: which colors represent which groups, how axis breaks and labels appear, and so on.


ggplot(viz_data, aes(x = outcome, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ group) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Outcome by treatment group", x = NULL, y = "Count")







Saving plots
Once you’re happy with a plot, ggsave() writes it to a file (PDF, PNG, JPEG, etc.), inferring the format from the file extension. It’s good practice to save plots into their own subfolder, created with dir.create() if it doesn’t already exist.

dir.create("plots", showWarnings = FALSE)

p <- ggplot(viz_data, aes(x = outcome, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ group) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("plots/outcome_by_group.pdf", plot = p, width = 8, height = 5)
